rationale: A wins because it treats Whatnot's $3B as a reporting problem, not a victory lap: "Whatnot says it hit $3B in live-auction sales. It won't say what sellers actually make" is the sharpest real story in either set. B has usable bones, but it keeps over-asserting the thing it needs to prove, especially in "The People Who Make a Living Running Live Auctions" and "Squeezing Resale's Incumbents." A has one ugly math stumble, but B has a confidence problem.
gaps_in_A: "A private company with $3B in sales and a $5B valuation is worth less than one times revenue it doesn't keep" gets the math/framing wrong: nearly $5B is not less than one times $3B, and GMV is explicitly not revenue.
"two of the most contested resale categories in retail" quietly turns fashion and electronics into resale categories, which the update does not state.

"the shutdown-and-retreat cycle of Western live-shopping efforts" is plausible context, but it is not in the supplied facts and should be labeled as outside proof needed, not treated as settled background.
gaps_in_B: "The People Who Make a Living Running Live Auctions" invents the core fact. The update says sellers run auctions, not that they make a living or use it as primary income.

"someone who goes live repeatedly each week selling trading cards or sneakers as a primary income source" piles on unsupplied color: repeat schedule, sneakers, and primary income all come from nowhere.
"Squeezing Resale's Incumbents" asserts market impact before proving overlap or loss. The set even admits the reporter will challenge this, which means the headline is ahead of the evidence.
The refused valuation angle is too timid: "Take-rate is undisclosed" is exactly why the GMV-versus-revenue/private-valuation question is interesting, not a reason to kill it outright.
